newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Stals dashes S.Africa market hopes with rate hike.
newsitem.headline: Stals dashes S.Africa market hopes with rate hike.

text.p: Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals on Wednesday dashed hopes South African markets might ride out a liquidity squeeze without an official rate increase, announcing a one point hike in the Bank rate to 17 percent.
Commercial banks are expected to follow suit with a similar one point hike in the prime lending rates to 20.25 percent on Thursday.
That will deal a fresh blow to an already stuttering South African economy and stock market, analysts said.
The increase in the Bank rate, effective from November 21, takes the rate at which the central bank to lends overnight to commercial banks to the highest level since early 1992.

The move took many analysts by surprise. There had been a widespread belief that Stals would resist market pressure for an official rate rise, at least until a clearer picture emerged on credit demand and money supply growth at the end of the month.
That view was given weight by reports this week that the central bank was in talks with commercial banks on ways to avert a rate increase.

"To an extent it was unexpected in that we thought the Reserve Bank wanted to let the markets sweat it out a little bit until they got hold of the next credit numbers," said Dennis Dykes, chief economist at Nedcor bank.
"But looking at it coldly with the rand still under pressure and credit demand still very high and the market shortage for this time of the month very high, it can't necessarily be criticised."
However, the move was condemned by the South African Chamber of Business (Sacob) which described it as a "severe blow" to the economy.
Hania Farhan, economist with ING Barings in Johannesburg, said it would further undermine 1997 growth prospects, unless reversed very quickly.
"If this higher interest rate carries on beyond the end of the year, we will definitely have to revise down our growth forecasts," she said.
Farhan is currently looking for growth of 2.7 percent next year, down from around 3.0 percent this year and a seven-year high of 3.3 percent achieved in 1995.
Other economists said it was possible rates might be cut again in the first half of next year, given indications that credit extension and consumer demand were already under pressure.

"I see this as a temporary situation and with the economy slowing down I think one can see a reversal, possibly quite early next year, if the rand stabilises at current levels," said Johan Louw, chief economist at life assurer Sanlam in Cape Town.

"I think we will have a rate cut in the second quarter of next year, perhaps a bit sooner...followed by another drop in the second half of next year. There is even the possibility there might be three (rate cuts) next year."

Nedcor's Dykes said the rate rise would clearly brake economic growth further next year -- which he was already expecting to be no more than two percent. But he said this should prove to be the peak of the interest rate cycle.
"I would think we will probably have a reduction in the first half of next year," he said.
Stals said the Bank rate increase, the second this year, was necessary given the instability of the rand, rising short- term money market rates and the threat of higher inflation.

Commercial banks have been squeezed by a severe money market shortage this month, averaging over nine billion rand a day, reflecting lack of funds due to renewed investor uncertainty in the face of further falls in the rand.
The currency has shed 22.2 percent of its value on a trade-weighted basis so far this year.
